Coffee came to India, the story goes, around 1670, when the Sufi saint Baba Budan carried seven coffee beans back from Yemen and planted them in the hills of Chikmagalur in Karnataka.

At the time Yemen controlled the world's coffee supply. Its port of Mocha shipped the beans, and growers were careful to export only roasted or boiled seeds that could not sprout. Baba Budan is said to have hidden fertile beans in his beard on his way home from the pilgrimage to Mecca. Seven is a sacred number in Islam. The range where he planted them is still called the Baba Budan Giri.

In the 1690s Dutch traders took seedlings from the Malabar coast to start coffee in Java, a key step in coffee spreading around the tropics. In the 19th century British planters cleared estates across Karnataka and Kerala, and also in Ceylon until coffee rust destroyed them.

Today India is a large coffee producer, and Karnataka grows most of it. The trail runs back to coffee in Yemen.
sum: Coffee came to India, the story goes, around 1670, when the Sufi saint Baba Budan carried seven coffee beans back from Yemen and planted them in the hills of Chikmagalur in Karnataka.
